Frequently Asked Questions


Does offline tracking stop the device from working as a Meshtastic node?

No. The modification adds local location caching while retaining normal Meshtastic communication, including position broadcasts and message reception. 


Does the tracker save a point every minute without a GPS location?

The automatic recording interval is one minute, but the device needs a GPS position available to save a location point. 


Why do deleted tracks return when I reconnect?

Deleting position history in the app does not remove the points cached on the device. Reconnecting allows the node to replay them. Clear the device cache if you no longer want those saved positions to return. 


Can I export tracks without the Meshtastic phone app?

Yes. The repository includes a Windows batch tool called tracker.bat that can export a GPX file without using the Meshtastic app.

title: Americans are warming to a healthcare idea that once seemed politically impossible
description:
Americans have hit a breaking point with health insurance.

Saddled with growing medical bills and totally reliant on stable jobs to stay healthy, the majority of Americans now say they would prefer a government plan that offers health insurance to everyone. 

Two-thirds of U.S. adults now support a national healthcare plan or “Medicare for All,” according to recent polling from health policy research group KFF. That’s a dramatic increase from 2020, when 53% of U.S. adults favored universal healthcare through a government plan, an option common among other wealthy nations. 

In the poll, 32% of respondents said they would “strongly favor” a single government healthcare plan that provides insurance for all Americans. An additional 34% of those polled said they would “somewhat favor” the overhaul to the U.S. healthcare system, with just 15% saying they “somewhat oppose” the idea and 19% saying they “strongly oppose” it. In the KFF poll, 84% of Democrats and 72% of independents were in favor of a national health insurance plan, compared with 34% of Republicans.

Another survey published this week by Axios-Ipsos confirmed the swell of support for reinventing the current U.S. healthcare system. In that poll, 43% of respondents said they would support a Medicare for All proposal that would replace the current private health insurance system. In that poll, 24% of respondents said they would oppose such a plan, while 32% reported being “unsure.” More Democrats (62%) and independents (47%) favored a government-run healthcare system, while a slight majority of Republicans opposed the idea (52%).

Crushing healthcare costs

Soaring support for a government-run health insurance system isn’t a mystery. Americans spend more on healthcare than people in other wealthy countries, but the U.S. government spends more, too—even without a broad national plan that insures everyone. Somehow all of that spending still adds up to worse health outcomes. In spite of spending twice what many of its peer countries spend per capita on healthcare, Americans live shorter, less healthy lives.

Americans are paying more and getting less when it comes to healthcare—and that spending is stretching them thin. In the richest country in the world by many measures, people are skipping doses of their meds and even buying less food to afford their rising healthcare costs. 

In the new Axios-Ipsos poll, 69% of Americans said they were worried about the rising cost of healthcare, with the same percentage reporting that a 10% increase in costs would hurt their family’s financial situation. A shocking 100 million Americans were already crushed under the weight of medical debt in 2022, and the situation is unlikely to improve given recent cuts to Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies. In 2024, Americans took out $74 billion in loans to pay their medical bills, with most borrowing more than $500.

U.S. voters fed up with the current state of health insurance will have a way to voice that displeasure soon. Progressive Democrats in some key November battleground races are running on a push for Medicare for All, but the party’s center and its leadership have yet to warm up to the idea in spite of soaring support among their constituents.

title: Healthcare has a churn problem
description:
I was diagnosed with anorexia at 10 years old. Over the next several years, my family and I navigated a healthcare system that was mostly focused on how many days I stayed in a hospital bed instead of whether I was getting better.

I spent my entire freshman year of high school in and out of facilities, counting down 45-minute therapy slots while fighting a brain disorder that forces you to battle your own mind upwards of six times a day. The bills came in, claims were processed, and the checkboxes were ticked, but I was still struggling with anorexia.

Decades later, now as a founder and CEO of an eating disorder treatment program, I realize my teenage experience embodied the traditional healthcare business model to a T.

THE ONLY INDUSTRY WHERE PRODUCT FAILURE IS PROFITABLE

In traditional healthcare, revenue is tied to volume: More time in session results in more revenue. The more appointments booked, the more the facility can bill; the longer someone stays in treatment—and the more times they relapse—the more profitable the facility becomes.

If any consumer tech or hardware startup ran on this model, it would fail fast. It’s like going to an auto repair shop that charges by the hour, sends you home with a car that still stalls, and then charges you again when you have to tow it back into the shop.

The main problem is industry alignment. Fee-for-service models reward visit volume and usually lead to fragmented, episodic care. Value-based outcome models, on the other hand, tie reimbursement directly to clinical and financial outcomes. If we want a healthcare system that can keep up with rising costs and demand, we need to align incentives around real, measurable outcomes.

BUILD WHAT WORKS

Tying financial compensation to real-world outcomes gives leaders the flexibility to build better products that result in positive outcomes for all parties involved. In healthcare, that means patients, their families, providers, and health insurance plans.

For example, when we started Equip, we knew that once-a-week therapy wasn’t enough to address a complex eating disorder, but the traditional fee-for-service billing system made it nearly impossible to bill for anything else. By partnering with forward-thinking health insurance plans to develop value-based payment structures, we designed the treatment model families needed: a team of doctors, dietitians, therapists, and coaches delivered virtually. This approach provides the right dose of care when patients need it, without uprooting their daily routines or stopping them from building a life worth living.

WHAT DOES “GOOD” LOOK LIKE?

The catch, however, is that the healthcare industry has historically lacked a consensus on what “good” means. Defining quality is particularly difficult in eating disorders, where recovery isn’t as simple as a blood test or a healed bone. The field uses two tools—the EDE-Q and the PARDI-AR—to set severity thresholds, but neither gets into what “getting better” means. It also requires a long-term view, which can clash with an industry where most health insurance plans operate on 12- to 24-month budget cycles.

When I was 10, that meant staying in a hospital bed long enough for my vitals to stabilize. But as I found out through many cycles of treatment, that didn’t lead to me getting better.

To solve the national mental health crisis, we need an economic framework where doing good and doing good business are the same. By replacing the traditional model with outcome-based partnerships, we aren’t just building more efficient companies, but delivering on healthcare’s biggest promise: building a product that works.

Kristina Saffran is cofounder and CEO of Equip.

title: AI fear is driving employees to slack off, show up late, and even steal coworkers’ lunches
description:
As more businesses adopt artificial intelligence, some employees—who are increasingly worried about losing their jobs—are starting to act out.

That’s the finding of a new study from Washington State University researchers, published in the journal Occupational Health Science, that looks at how AI adoption at work is affecting workers’ attitudes and behaviors in the office.

Research has shown that the increase of AI-based technologies at work—such as intelligent robotics, automated systems, and algorithmic management—may make employees feel insecure about their jobs and lead to more stress and less engagement.

Washington State University’s study looked at employees across 18 different industries and found that workers who had the greatest fears about being replaced by AI were more likely to behave poorly by, for example, slacking off at the office or even stealing a coworker’s lunch.

Researchers also found that employees who assumed they would be displaced were more likely to “morally disengage” at work, such as by coming in late for a shift or surfing the web while on the clock.

“Moral disengagement is basically a way of justifying bad behavior,” Tahira M. Probst, a professor of psychology at WSU Vancouver and lead author of the study, said in a news release. “We know what’s right and wrong. We know what organizational policies say we can and can’t do. Moral disengagement is a way of reframing that behavior as something that is acceptable.”

Researchers used the AI Industry Exposure index to identify which industries were most exposed to potential AI disruption. Workers in finance and insurance had some of the highest levels of exposure, while workers in agriculture, forestry, and construction had the least. Not surprisingly, the bad behavior was more pronounced in the industries with the highest amount of disruption.

The study’s bottom line: When employees feel their jobs are at risk, they may look at workplace expectations differently and rationalize behaviors such as cutting corners or undermining coworkers to protect themselves or compensate for what they perceive as injustice.

The findings also suggest that AI anxieties can hurt workers and businesses alike, pointing to the need for employers to be more mindful of how they roll out AI in the workplace so employees are better supported.

title: The hidden costs of fracking: boom in Argentina linked to trail of sickness
description:
Families in Vaca Muerta, the centre of Patagonia’s shale operation, report cancers, miscarriages and pollution

In Allen, a small town in Argentine Patagonia, many people living on the same street ended up falling ill. For some, it was severe migraines, nausea or skin irritation. For others, cancers, congenital abnormalities, miscarriages or stillbirth seemed to affect foetuses or children. People say it all started 13 years ago – when a well was drilled near their homes to extract gas and oil.

Calle Ciega 10 [Dead-end Street 10] lies on the eastern edge of Vaca Muerta, a vital area for Argentina’s economy, home to the world’s second-largest reserve of shale gas and fourth-largest reserve of shale oil. The region has more than 2,600 active wells, including one on this small street where about 20 families live, most of them seasonal workers on fruit farms.

At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports

Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

title: Azenya Villas / KWCA - Kosala Weerasekara Chartered Architects

Designed during the country's economic crisis, the project was driven by one idea: to keep construction costs as low as possible without compromising the experience of the place. The answer was a simple gabled form with a small footprint, extended vertically rather than spread across the land, and repeated to give the retreat a clear identity.

title: Century-old Isle of Wight fossil reveals Europe's first megaraptoran
description:
Researchers have identified a new predatory dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina, from a skull fragment found on the Isle of Wight, making it the first known megaraptoran found in Europe. The animal lived about 120 million years ago and was likely 3 to 4 metres long, with powerful forelimbs and curved claws estimated at 10 to 20 centimetres [sciencedaily.com#1][sci.news#1][cbsnews.com#2].

The Natural History Museum acquired the fossil in 1924, but it remained undescribed until a team led by University College London examined it. The discovery supports a proposed route in which megaraptorans spread from Asia through Europe to Gondwana, rather than reaching the southern continents by island-hopping. The researchers published the study in Royal Society Open Science on October 14, 2026 [sci.news#1][aawsat.com#1][sciencedaily.com#1].

title: Former ARPA-H director Renee Wegrzyn wants to solve science’s ‘magic hands’ problem
description:
Renee Wegrzyn spent her career building the future of American science—including the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, or ARPA-H, the White House agency created to accelerate health breakthroughs.

Then the Trump administration showed her the door. Wegrzyn cofounded Transfyr to tackle what she calls one of the most overlooked issues in science: the magic hands problem. She explains why fixing this unglamorous bottleneck is the prerequisite for everything AI promises to deliver in medicine, and why she can feel the next Sputnik moment coming—even if she can’t quite name it yet.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by Robert Safian, former editor-in-chief of Fast Company. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

You were at ARPA-H, the inaugural director of a White House effort to accelerate health research. You were amped up about the possibilities, but with the Trump administration, you had to pivot. Was it hard not to take it personally that they wanted different leadership?

I’ll tell you, I’m still amped up about it. It’s still an amazing idea. Obviously, DARPA [the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency] has been around for almost 80 years. I hope ARPA-H will have the same longevity and continue to live on today.

I’m a builder. I love to take things forward and really show what’s possible. So was it hard when I left? Of course it was hard. I had a really unusual appointment: I was a presidential appointee, but I was term-limited, so I served through the transition and had a few weeks in the new administration. I served in “Trump one,” by the way, as well.

So it was a great opportunity to make sure they really understood why we built the agency. We needed an ARPA-H because there was something missing in the way we were doing science broadly, which was: How do you move really quickly? How do you get focused on a problem versus building a general knowledge set? I was able to show them what we were building and convince them that it was worth keeping around. I couldn’t be more proud of the agency and its perseverance.

So your new business, Transfyr—The New York Times wrote about you, and the article kept referring to “magic hands.” I’m curious what magic hands are. What problem is Transfyr trying to solve or address?

You probably have your favorite dish, or your parents’ or grandparents’ favorite dish. Sometimes they just have the magic hands. Nobody can cook it like they do. Nobody can make it taste the special way they can. And that happens in science as well. There are some scientists who just have the knack and can deliver really great science over and over.

The challenge is that a lot of those scientists are such experts they can hardly describe what they’re doing. It’s an art in some ways. And so the magic hands idea was really a testament to what those scientists can do in the lab.

The pipeline we’re creating at Transfyr is: Can we create computer vision and perception tools to capture the work of science as it’s being done so that we understand, if the protocol says, “Mix the cells,” whether someone is inverting the tube in a certain gentle way, while another researcher may be rigorously shaking or vortexing it, which could destroy the sample?

Those little things, compounded over the many decisions a scientist may make over the course of several hours of experimentation, lead to what is called magic hands.

Was this an issue you saw at ARPA-H, the sort of breakthroughs that were trapped in a single lab in some ways?

Where that manifested at DARPA and at ARPA-H was in a realization, through my career, of how fragile breakthroughs are. Usually, the way a breakthrough is first communicated to the world is through a research publication, a Science or Nature paper. That paper is not a product. It’s not commercializable. It’s not ready for a patient that day. That’s the starting gun for what is going to happen.

The ARPAs of this world are really fantastic at getting to that initial breakthrough and demonstrating what is possible, but following through and delivering is not a 100% guaranteed activity.

When I started ARPA-H, we wanted customers, who would be the final users of that technology, to give us feedback on what we were developing so that when we got to the last day of the experiment, they were demanding that product, versus having that be the first contact with a customer, which unfortunately is pretty common around traditional grant-making organizations.

It’s rethinking how you make sure you can transfer that knowledge off the back end of a program.

Because the folks at the lab aren’t necessarily worrying about, or prioritizing, how to make it scalable. They’re just trying to see if it works. But of course, eventually we want it to be scalable.

Sometimes the folks in the lab don’t even have the expertise or understanding of who they need to talk to next to do that, right? We think about science and those transfers as handoffs. We deploy our technology to an originating lab to understand the science and what was important about that discovery, but we can also deploy it in a receiving lab so that we can see how they’re reproducing it.

And instead of the way we transfer science today, which is looking over each other’s shoulders and saying, “Oh, you’re doing it a little wrong,” we have this video-connectedness that lets us help accelerate those iterations of transferring the science.

Do you ever get frustrated about how resources are allocated in our world? You’ve put your life toward this work, and yet so much money is devoted to, I don’t know, space exploration or the next hot social app, the Meta Muse craze. How do you deal with government and how it prioritizes things?

Yeah, it’s maddening. One of the things that has me nervous right now is that I look back on the last 80 years following the Second World War. We’ve led the globe in science and engineering and innovation. Nobody who’s practicing science today has practiced science in the United States at a time when we weren’t, quote-unquote, winning from a competitiveness perspective, when we weren’t at the top.

I genuinely believe we may lose that competitiveness, that edge, that incumbency, and I’m not sure I see us fighting for it in the way that we should be. We have to deliver on what we’ve promised to do, and that’s a commitment not just to my country, but to my kids and my family. 

What I think a lot about is Sputnik moments. We’re going to look back at this moment in time like there’s something happening, and it’s going to impact whatever’s happening 20 to 50 years from now. You can feel it in the moment.

Where that happened before, of course, was Sputnik. The United States didn’t know the Soviet Union was developing that capability, and we didn’t have a counter-capability. What I realized is that each individual person has a Sputnik moment in their life that is usually health-related. My Sputnik moment was when my mother was diagnosed with cancer. That stopped everything.

Everybody has a story, whether it happened to them or their family, or if you talk to a member of Congress, something’s happening in their state that they can’t deal with.

So I’m like, “What is the Sputnik moment now?” If ARPA-H was bringing people from an unhealthy state to a healthy state, what’s happening now is taking us beyond that. If we can figure out and solve health and wellness, a lot of people talk about abundance. What is the next trajectory? What is the Sputnik that we’re working toward?

title: FBI arrests and investigates this OpenAI engineer over a ‘sophisticated listening device’
description:
An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

—Eric Tucker, Associated Press

title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
description: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

title: From black soldier flies to mealworms: farming insects for food, fodder and fertiliser in Uganda
description:
Cultivating the nutritious bugs means families can raise livestock and enrich their own food, while lowering pressures on the land

A few minutes’ walk from his home in the Kyaka II refugee settlement, Kanane Bikanyale feeds black soldier fly larvae to chickens in a coop above a fishpond. The larvae disappear in a scrum of chickens. Nearby, more larvae grow in modified jerrycans, while adult flies are kept in netted boxes.

Bikanyale kept chickens before he fled to Uganda from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). But the cost of conventional feed and shortages of ingredients made them increasingly difficult to raise – a widespread pressure for millions of smallholder farmers whose margins are tight.

title: Learning Through Practice: Why Architecture Students Enter Competitions
description: On paper, entering an architecture competition is one of the most challenging things an architecture student can do. What draws students to them is the chance to experiment, approaching a loosely defined program that leaves room to test unconventional ideas and unfamiliar tools outside the rhythm of the semester. That distance from assessment is a relatively recent development, as competitions were once central to architectural education.

Also on the radar are the winning proposal for Itaú Cultural's new headquarters on Avenida Paulista, international recognition for two Brazilian landscape architecture projects, and a national diagnosis highlighting persistent gaps in pedestrian infrastructure and road safety.

title: Beyond the Box: What Shipping Container Architecture Gets Right and Where It Falls Short
description: Using shipping containers as the basis for a structure—also known as "cargotecture"—seems like a simple approach to building. Perhaps deceptively so. While it's true that containers are a quick, cost-effective, and often low-effort building material, and that they're durable and customizable, container conversions also bring their challenges. Without careful planning, the build process can be painful and the results underwhelming.

title: Making Room for Water: Floodable Parks in Latin America
description: Walk along a river in almost any Latin American city and you will find stretches that have been straightened, lined with concrete, buried beneath roads, or pushed behind industrial areas and residential neighborhoods. Throughout the twentieth century, urban expansion gradually occupied riverbanks and former floodplains, while waterways were redirected or confined within infrastructure intended to control them. Yet the water continued to return. For decades, flooding has been the most frequent natural disaster in Latin America and the Caribbean, according to the Inter-American Development Bank.

title: NASA's Perseverance rover drives 45.22 kilometers, sets off-world record
description:
NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles) on Mars, surpassing the 45.16-kilometer record held by the Opportunity rover, NASA said. Perseverance passed the mark on Oct. 11, its 2,006th Martian day, after about five and a half years on the planet; Opportunity took nearly 15 years to cover its distance [nasa.gov#1][sci.news#1][npr.org#1].

The rover reached the milestone while traveling toward Idubi through Lac de Charmes, near the western rim of Jezero Crater. Perseverance has collected 29 rock and soil samples and found a potential biosignature in a river-channel rock; the finding does not prove that ancient life existed on Mars [astrobiology.com#1][timeslive.co.za#1]. The crater rim may also preserve evidence of ancient hydrothermal systems, including warm or hot groundwater [dawn.com#1].

NASA has extended the rover’s mission through about the end of 2028 to continue exploring the crater rim. The vehicle’s original driving target was about 20 kilometers, and engineers are testing its mobility systems for a possible total range of 100 kilometers or more [sci.news#1][dawn.com#1]. The samples’ eventual return to Earth remains uncertain, NPR reported, citing the program’s cost and concerns raised by planetary geologist Philip Christensen [npr.org#1].

description:
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic reportedly offered a salary of 145,000 euros (roughly equal to $190,000) for a personal assistant in its London office.

The posting called for a “highly organized, detail-oriented, and self-starting administrative business partner” to support “senior go-to-market” leaders. Responsibilities would include scheduling, “handling travel logistics,” managing an executive’s inbox and communications, filing expense claims, and other office tasks.

The post, since removed from Anthropic’s website but preserved here, also stated that the role would require “outstanding attention to detail, strong relationship-building skills, and the ability to anticipate needs across teams while ensuring responsive, error-free execution.”

Fast Company reached out to Anthropic for comment.

Social media users are pointing to the apparent irony of a leading agentic AI firm hiring a human worker to do a job that an AI agent could, at least theoretically, largely handle.

“Somebody should really build some sort of tech tool that can handle this stuff autonomously,” one user quipped.

title: 3 leadership lessons from AI-powered companies
description:
Even as AI investment rises, many organizations don’t see the returns they expected. They might see small improvements by deploying AI tools into existing structures. But true success means thinking beyond the technology alone, reinventing tomorrow’s workflows, and putting AI to work for people. Our research shows only 5% of organizations are redesigning work, while others are optimizing what already exists.

When my role evolved to blend people leadership with AI enablement, it sent a clear message from our CEO: AI requires a strong people strategy at the core. I’ve seen real transformation when organizations bet on people, not just AI.

The companies unlocking results are asking the right questions about how work should change. What those leaders are learning comes down to a few key steps.

BUILD THE FOUNDATION ON DATA AND GOVERNANCE

When we rebuilt our AI HR operating model at ServiceNow, we considered how we would design it if we were starting from scratch. That helped us move from scattered pilots to a structured process with clear governance, accountability, and a way to scale without chaos.

PepsiCo’s executive vice president and chief people officer, Becky Schmitt, took a similar, structured approach. In a webinar we hosted, Schmitt a client of ours shared how she focused on data hygiene and prioritized all employees, including frontline and factory employees where safety and wellbeing are nonnegotiable.

With clean data and transparent definitions, employees can better trust and verify what AI tells them. When trust grows, adoption accelerates.

“As we’ve thought about what it means to adopt AI and harness the full power of this technology, we have five principles. Everything is human-centered. We’re fair, transparent, we have accountability, and we’re safe from the start,” she said.  

When roles are clear and processes are simple, people move faster and smarter. Governance builds confidence.

ENABLE YOUR PEOPLE WITH SKILLS THAT MATTER

By 2031, the fastest-growing technical skills will be linked to data quality, software development, analytics, and AI, according to our research. But demand for distinctly human capabilities is also accelerating.

This dual reality changes how we should think about enablement. Our client, Omar Abbosh, chief executive officer at Pearson, studies these dynamics closely. In another webinar we hosted, he said key skills that matter now are agency, learning velocity, and emotional intelligence.

Add adaptability and design thinking, and people can evolve faster than the environment shifts.

“We need to rewire occupations. We need to understand where you apply agents to specific tasks, how agents work with people, and how people can supervise and orchestrate. That level of rewiring results in a new operating model. It’s process, it’s systems, and it’s the motivation required to change the culture,” he said in the webinar.

But you can’t teach these skills in a classroom. Real-time learning embedded in daily work beats traditional reskilling programs. We give our employees personalized learning recommendations tailored to how AI will be used in their roles, which allows them to understand the why behind its use and the value of human judgment in their work. We have seen that when you coach people through the work they’re doing, learning is faster, stickier, and more scalable.

TRANSFORM THE WORKFORCE WITH CHANGE READINESS 

AI adoption is increasing, yet many people aren’t aware of their organization’s AI strategy. This is a disconnect that leaders need to address with continuous, adaptive, and decentralized change readiness.

This is often the hardest part of a transformation because it’s complex and abstract. It’s about changing the way we work at a fundamental level, which requires a strong understanding of your organization’s structure and capabilities. And it requires keeping employees informed about the skills the organization is prioritizing, how roles are evolving, and the path forward.

Another client of ours, Nickle LaMoreaux, senior vice president and chief human resources officer at IBM, used an “X-Ray” framework as a foundation to rethink her organization with an AI-native mindset. As she explained in a different webinar we hosted, “We were really clear from the beginning that we were going to put employees at the center of this.”

By recognizing the importance of redesigning jobs and helping employees feel comfortable with the technology, Nickle built a powerful model to map current skills against future needs.

Her team also identified where redesign was most urgent. Then, IBM shared that analysis with employees.

“You have to redesign jobs. If you wait too long, you can quickly fall behind, especially at the pace things are moving today. When we talk about redesigning jobs, we need to shift our thinking from the job as a whole to the tasks and skills underneath it,” she said.

That kind of analysis can help leaders think about future skills as AI changes work. The end goal is a workforce that can pivot at the speed of innovation. It’s about shifting the mindset to “let’s try this” instead of “don’t break this.”

THE FLYWHEEL

We’ve been through big technology shifts before. AI transformation feels different because of the pace, but those examples should give us confidence.

Each step creates the conditions for the next. They can help us shift from talking about change to showing people what it feels like when their roles evolve to expand their potential.

For leaders, this is the moment to put people at the center, powered by technology and a clear plan. In my experience, that has always been the right combination.

Jacqui Canney is the chief people and AI enablement officer at ServiceNow.

title: The Key to Multilingualism Lies in the Ears, Not the Mouth
description:
Steve Martin’s favorite comic moment of his entire career is the “hamburger” scene from The Pink Panther (2006), he once told People magazine. Martin plays Inspector Clouseau, who has an aggressively exaggerated French accent. In the scene, he is trying to learn how to say, “I would like to buy a hamburger,” with a dialect coach. “Dam-buergaaaaa,” he purrs at his coach, along with increasingly ridiculous permutations of all of the other words in the sentence.

The scene is funny because it’s true for so many of us: Learning a new language as an adult can be hard. The unfamiliar sounds may get tangled up in the mouth like marbles, and the results can sound like gibberish. But for other people, new foreign words seem to roll off the tongue and adopting different accents comes easily. Their secret may lie in how they listen, according to a new study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology. People who are better at detecting small differences in the frequency of raw sound are better at picking up new foreign speech sounds, and thus might be quicker to learn new languages, the study found.

“Read more: Speaking More Languages May Help Slow Brain Aging”

The post The Key to Multilingualism Lies in the Ears, Not the Mouth appeared first on Nautilus.

Poor sleep and unhealthy eating habits, meanwhile, were linked to lower flexibility and resilience.

title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
description:
Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift

A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.

The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.

title: Built-in Agility and the Architecture of the Infinite Lifecycle
description: While architecture often responds to a specific program of uses, taking into account areas, contexts, and various economic and technical conditions, buildings rarely remain the same throughout their lifespan. Programs, spatial dynamics, and users' needs change, as do environmental, economic, and technological conditions, requiring interventions that were likely not anticipated at the beginning of a project. Steel structures make it possible to envision architecture capable of growing, transforming, being disassembled, and reassembled. Their dimensional precision, industrialized components, and potential for mechanical connections enable the design of open systems prepared for future interventions.
